$Comment: What Trim Work is worth. This is the wage: it always pays, and it pays more the
further along the woodcutter is. Trim Work names three other tables beside this one, so keep
this file about the wage alone and retune tools, finds and the kit where they live.
THE FIRST ROLL IS A LADDER. Its Factors are summed into one score and the Floors are read
against that score. Floors are NOT cumulative: the highest one reached wins and only its Grants
fire. Two things feed the score, weighted equally: the Woodcutting level, so the wage grows with
the skill, and Woodcutting luck, so a luck-heavy tree pays here as well as at the bench.
WHERE THE FLOORS SIT. The quest that opens Trim Work asks for a Woodcutting level first, so in
an ordinary game the twenty-five floor is the lowest anybody stands on and the ones above it are
the real ladder. The top floor wants both halves of the score well along rather than one alone.
THE ZERO FLOOR IS A SAFETY NET, and worth keeping even though it looks unreachable. A ladder
grants NOTHING when every floor sits above the worker's score, so if a score ever comes in lower
than the quest's own gate implies, a level reset, a server that has re-tuned what the quest asks,
a wallet of luck that reads zero, the run would otherwise pay nothing at all. It is written low
on purpose: it is a floor under the floor, not a tier anybody is meant to sit on.
UNITS, the one trap worth knowing. Both channels are read as WHOLE NUMBERS: MMO_Luck_WOODCUTTING
stores whole percent points, so a fully claimed Woodcutting tree reads near a hundred rather
than near one, and MMO_Level_WOODCUTTING is a level, not a fraction. The floors are therefore
written on a scale of roughly twenty-five to two hundred and sixty, the ceiling a capped level
with a full tree, the trophy hatchet in hand and the woodcutter's kit worn. Never swap these two
leaves for the mmoskilltree:station_luck aggregate: that one returns a FRACTION, which would
shift every floor by a factor of a hundred, and composing it beside a luck channel counts the
same investment twice.
RANGES. Amount with AmountMax pays experience drawn evenly between the two, and Count with
CountMax does the same for a stack, each decided once when the payout is. That is what keeps two
runs at the same tier from reading identically. Widen a pair to make a run swingier, or set
the two halves equal to make a line pay a flat number again.
THE SECOND ROLL is the same ladder again behind a coin flip, paying a smaller slice of
experience and nothing else. Rolls evaluate INDEPENDENTLY, so on about half of runs it lands on
top of the wage and the run reads as a good one. It carries no Cue on purpose: the wage has
already been announced, and a second chime for a top-up is noise.
The byproducts widen with the tier rather than simply growing: fibre and bark at every floor,
sap from the second, sticks from the third, which is what makes a higher tier feel like a
different run rather than a bigger number.

Rolls.$Comment: The wage. Always pays, at exactly one of the five floors.

Floors.$Comment: The safety net, under the level the quest itself asks for. A score can only land here if something outside this table put the worker below it, and a run still pays.
The starting tier: a woodcutter who has only just earned the order.
Past the early levels, or a few luck rewards claimed. Sap starts here.
A committed woodcutter: a solid level with real luck behind it. Sticks start here.
The top of the ladder, wanting both halves of the score near their ceiling.

Rolls.$Comment: A good run: the same ladder behind a coin flip, paying a slice of experience on top of the wage and nothing else.

Floors.$Comment: The same safety net as the wage ladder's, so a score below the quest's own gate still gets the top-up rather than silently nothing.
